title: Bank-aware thread mapping and KV staging experiments
body:
Summary:
This note captures a set of CUDA kernel experiments that explore bank-aware thread/block mapping for FlashAttention-style fused attention and cooperative staging of paged KV shards into SM-local shared memory using cp.async. The goal is to increase sustained throughput for very long contexts (>= 4k tokens) while keeping 99th-percentile latency under target for interactive workloads. This is experimental — results are preliminary but show promising tradeoffs when avoiding shared-memory bank conflicts and co-designing the eviction/staging policy with thread mapping.

Motivation & problem statement:
- Paged KV lets us keep large contexts without OOM, but kernel performance is sensitive to how we stage pages into SM memory. Naive staging causes bank conflicts and strided L2 access patterns.
- FlashAttention-like fused softmax/attn kernels are memory-bandwidth-limited for long sequences; shared-memory contention further degrades throughput.
- Existing placement uses canonical lane->bank mapping that creates hot banks when kernel tiles are rectangular and sequence lengths align poorly with bank stride.

Design hypotheses:
1) Re-mapping thread lanes across banks (bank-aware thread mapping) reduces conflict-induced serialization and increases effective SM throughput for fused ops.
2) Using cp.async to bulk-transfer paged-KV tiles into padded shared memory combined with cooperative groups yields lower per-token latency vs single-thread prefetch loops.
3) Adding a small per-SM staging buffer and lightweight eviction hints allows us to overlap KV page loads across SMs and reduce tail latency spikes when multiple warps load the same page.

Kernel sketch (high level):
- Launch config: blockDim.x = 256 (4 warps), blockDim.y = variable (tile rows). We experiment with 128/256/512 lane blocks.
- Pre-stage: one warp performs cp.async from global (paged-KV) into smem region with padding to avoid bank conflicts (pad = 32 bytes per row).
- Remap: logical lane l maps to physical bank = (l * prime) % 32 where prime chosen to distribute contiguous loads across banks. Avoid direct l % 32 mapping for rectangular tiles.
- Fusion: when all cp.async commits complete, perform fused scale -> softmax -> dropout -> writeback into output buffer. Softmax reduction performed in two phases using warp shuffles and small smem partial sums.
- Writeback: fused write writes both the attention outputs and an optional compressed/quantized KV fragment back to a paging-friendly layout so subsequent requests hit cache lines nicely.

Bank-aware mapping notes:
- Observed bank conflict patterns when seq_len is a multiple of 64 or 128; the canonical mapping causes two or three banks to be targeted by many lanes.
- Using a coprime remapping (e.g., multiply by 13 then mod 32) spreads accesses across banks. For triangular attention tiles we rotate remap per tile row to avoid persistent hot banks.
- Padding rows by 8 or 16 bytes reduces residual conflict for small tiles; cost is small compared to avoiding serial bank accesses.

Staging & eviction heuristics:
- Staging buffer per-SM (configurable: 8–32KB) to hold 1–4 KV tile rows. If eviction pressure low, keep last-used pages pinned.
- Eviction hints are emitted by kernel: when an SM is likely to reuse the page within X tokens, it sets a reuse bit in a compact per-page metadata table in L2-friendly memory. A background tracer (GPU-side cooperative kernel or host-side logic) can then deprioritize eviction for hot pages.
- Tradeoff: larger staging buffer increases occupancy pressure; must tune tile height to maintain >50% occupancy for H100/A100.

Use of cp.async and async copy patterns:
- cp.async shows clear gains when transferring contiguous shards (reduced load latency + pagewalk entropy), but alignment matters. Ensure src pointers aligned to 128B.
- We chain cp.async + cp.async.commit + cp.async.wait to overlap global loads with compute and avoid stalling. For very small tiles (<128B) cp.async overhead dominates; fall back to ld.global for small rows.

TensorCore / WMMA observations:
- For fused matmul phases that are 16-bit friendly, using Tensor Cores yields 1.6–2.1x compute speedup on H100 for the matmul portion. However, the end-to-end benefit is gated by memory staging; faster matmul exposes more bank conflicts unless mapping is fixed.
- We experiment with mixed-precision (FP16/FP8) for KV storage; FP8 provides size wins but requires careful dequant on the fly (adds compute and increases shared-memory usage).

Profiling & measurement methodology:
- Hardware: A100 80GB (PCIe), H100 SXM.
- Tools: nsight systems (nsys) for timeline; nvprof for instruction stats (legacy), nvtx markers in kernels for slice granularity.
- Key metrics: tokens/s, tail latency (p99), SM occupancy, achieved shared-memory bandwidth (measured via counters), bank-conflict stalls (special perf counters), L2 read/write bytes.
- Bench patterns: batch sizes {1,4,8}, seq lens {512,2048,8192}, kv-widths {64,128,256}. Measurements averaged over 200 runs; median and p99 reported.

Representative microbench results (preliminary):
- Baseline (canonical mapping, no cp.async): batch=4, seq=8192, kv=128 -> 122 tokens/s, p99=420ms
- Bank-aware mapping + cp.async staging: same config -> 144 tokens/s (+18%), p99=320ms (-24%)
- With staging buffer tuned (pad=16B) and minor warp fusion: 154 tokens/s (+26%), p99=280ms (-33%)
- TensorCore-enabled matmul + bank-aware mapping: 178 tokens/s (+46% vs baseline), p99=310ms (slightly higher due to more eviction pressure)
Notes: results vary by run; improvements largest for long contexts and wider KV widths. Small sequences (<512) see minimal gains and sometimes regress slightly due to cp.async overhead.

Latency tail mitigation:
- Strategy: fast-path kernel for interactive requests (batch=1) with smaller tile height and no cp.async, and background stage large-page warmers that prefetch hot KV pages into L2 before requests arrive.
- Canary: measure observed p99 on prod-like traces to set threshold for when to flip to fast-path.

Engineering tradeoffs & ops considerations:
- Complexity: bank-aware mapping plus per-SM staging increases kernel complexity and maintenance cost. Driver updates and CUDA version differences may alter bank count/behavior.
- Portability: the remap strategy must be parameterized per-arch (A100 vs H100) — bank count, cp.async semantics, and maximum smem vary.
- Observability: expose per-request counters (eviction hits, prefetch misses, bank_conflict_ticks) via nvtx and host-visible counters to help ops tune staging parameters.

Open questions and unknowns:
- How stable are bank-conflict reductions across CUDA versions and future GPUs with different bank sizes? Need cross-version testing.
- Could a kernel-side adaptive remapper (runtime learns conflict pattern and switches prime multiplier) outperform static primes? Memory for telemetry might be expensive.
- Interaction with scheduling: when many SMs concurrently stage the same page, we see L2 hotspots. Need global page-use coordination or staggered staging across CTA launch offsets.

Next steps / experiments to run:
1) Implement dynamic prime selection: collect per-tile conflict counters and swap mapping every N iterations. Measure churn overhead.
2) Evaluate staging buffer sizes at scale (multi-GPU) with our simulator to understand cross-SM L2 pressure.
3) Add tiny page-warming kernel launched opportunistically between user requests for PLG workloads to reduce cold-start tails.
4) Add telemetry counters and a short-lived dashboard for A/B test observed p99 on the hosted fleet.

Appendix: useful commands and profiling knobs
- nsys timeline: nsys profile --output=bankmap-8192 --trace=cuda,osrt ./bench --seq 8192 --batch 4
- nvprof-style counters (legacy): nvprof --metrics dram__cycles_elapsed.avg,sm__pipe_cycles_active.avg ./bench
- nvcc flags used: -arch=sm_90 -lineinfo -O3 -Xptxas -v -gencode=arch=compute_80,code=sm_80 (tune per GPU)
- Notes on cp.async alignment: ensure base pointer % 128 == 0 and use cudaMallocPitch for page-aligned allocations where possible.

References and links:
- Internal PR with prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rw-infer/pull/2142

End of note. Please comment inline with profiling traces (nvtx ranges) and any unusual p99 patterns you observe on different CUDA toolchain versions.
